newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japanese semiconductor chiefs to cooperate.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japanese semiconductor chiefs to cooperate.

text.p: The chiefs of some of the world's biggest computer chip companies agreed at an industry summit on Friday to cooperate on developing next-generation chipmaking technologies and to push for more international intellectual property protection.

The executives also agreed to set up a task force to study how best to measure international semiconductor trade and market share figures. The U.S., Europe, Korea and Japan depend on trade data to gauge whether their semiconductor industries have fair access to the other's markets.

The executives met at the first session of the Semiconductor Council, an international industry association set up last August to discuss trade issues. The day-long meeting at a resort hotel 20 miles outside Honolulu was "cordial" and "productive," participants said.

"It's very significant that we could get this much done in the first meeting," said Pat Weber, vice chairman of Texas Instruments Inc, and one of the representatives of the U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association. "There's been a lot of cooperation recently."

Cooperation between American and Japanese semiconductor industries is something relatively new. Semiconductor trade was one of the biggest sources of conflict between Washington and Tokyo in the 1980s.
Under pressure from the U.S. government, Japan signed an agreement in 1986, and another in 1991, to increase the share of foreign semiconductor companies within the Japanese market to 20 percent.
Japan had achieved that goal by 1996, when the second agreement expired. So Japanese trade representatives argued at a Vancouver conference in August that there was no need for another agreement.
Instead of a formal trade agreement, American and Japanese semiconductor executives set up the Semiconductor Council to resolve their trade issues.

Earlier this year, the Korean and European semiconductor industry associations asked to join the council. They were formally admitted on Friday. The four members account for 90 percent of the world's chip production.

The industry associations also agreed to help each other in developing standard equipment to manufacture and process 12-inch silicon wafers -- the slabs of electrical material from which computer chips are made.
Currently, most chip producers use eight-inch wafers. Switching to 12-inch wafers requires the companies to each build entirely new billion-dollar factories.

"By collaborating as an industry, we believe we can reduce the total cost to any one company and accelerate delivering better technology," said Curtis Crawford, president of the chip unit of Lucent Technologies Inc, and a Semiconductor Council co-chair.
Council members agreed to eliminate tariffs on semiconductor products within two years, to protect each other's intellectual property and to study ways to reduce industry waste.
Still to be resolved is how the countries will measure each other's market share, which is vital to gauging whether their voluntary trade agreements are working.

At issue is how the industry associations will gather accurate market data without exposing sensitive competitive information, said Hajime Sasaki, senior executive vice president of Japan's NEC Corp and chairman of the Semiconductor Council.
The U.S. also does not want sales from U.S.-based arms of Japanese companies back to Japan to be counted as trade.
The council agreed to set up a task force to study trade-measurement issues. It could be months before the task force completes the study, executives said.
